title: The Vineyard, the Woes and the Lion
introduction: Isaiah 5 moves in three steps. It begins with a love song about a vineyard (verses 1 to 7), continues with six “woes” against the sins of the people (verses 8 to 25), and ends with a foreign army that comes like a lion to take its prey (verses 26 to 30). Read together, these three steps tell one single story: God gives a lot, His people give back bad fruit, and when His protection is removed, judgment comes.
finalWord: Where is the fruit that God is looking for?

points.title: The Vineyard: A Song That Becomes a Mirror
points.text:
“Let me sing for my beloved my love song concerning his vineyard: My beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill. He dug it and cleared it of stones, and planted it with choice vines; he built a watchtower in the midst of it, and hewed out a wine vat in it; and he looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes.” (Isaiah 5:1 and 2)

In ancient Israel, agriculture was not only a job but a language that everybody understood. Everyone knew how much effort it took to plant a vineyard on the rocky hills of Judah: you had to remove the stones, build a wall, raise a watchtower and cut a winepress into the rock. So when Isaiah describes a farmer who did all of this, his listeners immediately understand that this man did everything possible for his vineyard.

The chapter begins like a love song or a work song, and that is the secret of its power. If Isaiah had stood in the public square and shouted, “You are sinners and God is going to destroy you,” the people would simply have walked away. But by singing a story about a friend and his ungrateful vineyard, he lowers the defenses of his audience, and he even invites them to judge the case: “judge between me and my vineyard. What more was there to do for my vineyard, that I have not done in it?” (5:3 and 4). The listeners feel sorry for the farmer and think, “What an injustice, that vineyard is useless, he should destroy it.”

Then, exactly when the people are nodding their heads, Isaiah turns the mirror toward them: “For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” (5:7). The verse ends with a play on words that is very strong in Hebrew: God looked for mishpāṭ (justice) but found mispāḥ (bloodshed), He looked for ṣĕdāqâ (righteousness) but heard ṣĕʿāqâ (a cry of pain). The words sound almost the same, but they mean the opposite, just like a vineyard that looks good from far away but produces sour and rotten grapes. This is the same method the prophet Nathan used with King David in 2 Samuel 12, when he told him a story about a rich man who stole a poor man’s lamb, and after David condemned the man, Nathan said to him, “You are the man.” When direct preaching no longer works, God uses a story that enters through a side door.

Application: Has God ever spoken to us in such an unexpected way that we did not see the message coming? Sometimes He uses a story, a song, a conversation, a difficult situation or even the words of a child, and suddenly we realize that the message was for us. Jesus said that if His disciples were silent, “the very stones would cry out” (Luke 19:40), which shows that God is never short of ways to make His truth heard. We must always test these moments by Scripture, because God never contradicts His Word, but we must also keep our hearts open, because sometimes the message that changes us arrives through a door we were not watching.
points.alt: A symbolic engraving of a grower holding disappointing grapes in a carefully prepared Judean vineyard with a stone wall, watchtower and wine vat.

points.title: The Woes: Comfort That Silences Compassion
points.text:
“Woe to those who join house to house, who add field to field, until there is no more room, and you are made to dwell alone in the midst of the land.” (Isaiah 5:8)

“Woe to those who rise early in the morning, that they may run after strong drink, who tarry late into the evening as wine inflames them! They have lyre and harp, tambourine and flute and wine at their feasts, but they do not regard the deed of the LORD, or see the work of his hands.” (Isaiah 5:11 and 12)

In this second part, Isaiah stops singing and starts reading the charges. While the poor were losing their land because of debts, the rich were buying house after house and field after field, until there was no space left for anyone else. This was not only economic injustice, it was a direct violation of the law of God, because in Leviticus 25:23 God says, “the land is mine,” and the land of every family was supposed to stay with that family through the generations. The rich were taking for themselves what God had given to others.

At the same time, the leaders lived in endless parties with music and wine, from early in the morning until late at night. The mention of the drunkards shows a tragic irony, because verse 13 says, “Therefore my people go into exile for lack of knowledge; their honored men go hungry, and their multitude is parched with thirst.” The nation was spiritually dry and about to face judgment, drought and exile, while its leaders were anesthetized, drowning in expensive wine and completely disconnected from the pain of their own people and from the reality of God. Verse 12 gives the deepest diagnosis: they “do not regard the deed of the LORD.” The prophet Amos describes the same sickness when he speaks of the leaders who drink wine from bowls “but are not grieved over the ruin of Joseph” (Amos 6:6).

Application: Sin does not only change our behavior, our habits and the shape of our personality, it also takes away our ability to feel empathy and to show mercy. The leaders of Judah did not wake up one day and decide to stop caring about the poor. Little by little, their comfort and their pleasures made them unable to see the suffering around them. This is one of the most dangerous effects of sin, because a person who is anesthetized does not feel pain, but he also does not feel the pain of others, and he does not notice that his own life is in danger.
points.alt: A symbolic engraving of leaders absorbed in wine and music while a vulnerable family leaves with its belongings beyond the doorway.

points.title: The Lion: When the Wall Falls
points.text:
“He will raise a signal for nations far away, and whistle for them from the ends of the earth; and behold, quickly, speedily they come!... Their roaring is like a lion, like young lions they roar; they growl and seize their prey; they carry it off, and none can rescue.” (Isaiah 5:26 and 29)

At the end of the chapter, Isaiah shows what happens when a vineyard is left without walls: the wild animals come in. In verse 5, God had already said about His vineyard, “I will remove its hedge, and it shall be devoured; I will break down its wall, and it shall be trampled down.” Now in verses 26 to 30 we see who comes through that broken wall. God simply whistles, as a shepherd calls his animals, and a nation from far away comes running. The text does not give the name of the nation, but historically it points to the Assyrian empire, which invaded the land some years later. Isaiah describes its soldiers as tireless, with sharp arrows and horses with hooves like stone (5:27 and 28), and finally he compares them to a lion. The Hebrew word lābîʾ in verse 29 is translated by some versions as “lioness,” the hunter that seizes its prey and carries it away while no one is able to rescue it.

The connection between the three parts of the chapter is very logical. In the first act, God removes the protecting wall because the vineyard did not give good fruit. In the second act, the people are too drunk, too blind and too proud to notice that they are no longer protected. In the third act, the foreign predator walks in through the broken wall and devours the sleeping prey. Even the clouds connect the beginning and the end of the chapter, because in verse 6 God commands the clouds not to give rain to the vineyard, and in verse 30 the light is darkened by the clouds over the land.

Isaiah puts all of this together in one single chapter to shake his audience. He moves from the soft tone of a guitar around a campfire (the song of the vineyard), to the hard tone of a prosecutor reading the charges (the woes and the insensitivity of the leaders), and he ends with the sound of the boots of an invading army and the roar of a lion about to attack. It is a master class in literary tension.

Application: This progression makes us think about the “evil day” in the Christian life, which Paul mentions in Ephesians 6:13 when he tells us to put on the armor of God “that you may be able to withstand in the evil day.” Life can move very fast from the campfire song to the roar of the lion, and the person who lives anesthetized, like the leaders of Point 2, will not be ready when that day comes. That is why Peter writes, “Be sober minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5:8). In Isaiah the lion is an instrument of the judgment of God, while in Peter the lion is the enemy of our souls, but the lesson is the same: the sober and watchful person is not taken by surprise. And there is good news here too, because in Isaiah 5:29 the prey is carried away and “none can rescue,” but Jesus says about His sheep, “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28). In Christ, the wall that protects us cannot be broken.
points.alt: A symbolic engraving of a lioness entering a neglected vineyard through its broken wall, with an approaching army beneath dark clouds in the distance.

points.title: The Vineyard and the Son: Jesus’ Parable of the Tenants
points.text:
Jesus used this same image in the famous Parable of the Wicked Tenants (Matthew 21:33 to 46, Mark 12:1 to 12 and Luke 20:9 to 19), and He set up an ambush even sharper than the one of Isaiah. Jesus knew that the Pharisees and the chief priests knew Isaiah 5 by memory, so He used their own knowledge of the Bible as a perfect trap in three steps.

1. The Bait: the same beginning. Jesus starts His story saying, “There was a master of a house who planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a winepress in it and built a tower” (Matthew 21:33). These are almost the same words as Isaiah 5:2, so the religious leaders immediately recognized the song of the vineyard and probably thought they already knew where the story was going.

2. The Trap: they pronounce their own sentence. But this time the story changes. The problem is not the vineyard, which is good, but the tenants who were supposed to take care of it. They beat and kill the servants the owner sends, and finally they kill his own son (21:35 to 39). Then Jesus asks them the same kind of question that Isaiah asked in 5:3: “When therefore the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?” And they answer without hesitation, “He will put those wretches to a miserable death and let out the vineyard to other tenants who will give him the fruits in their seasons” (21:40 and 41). Just like David with Nathan, they condemn themselves with their own mouths.

3. The Turn: “You are the tenants.” Then Jesus quotes Psalm 118:22, “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone,” and says to them, “the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people producing its fruits” (21:42 and 43). Matthew tells us that “they perceived that he was speaking about them” (21:45). In Isaiah, the guilty one was the whole vineyard, but in the parable of Jesus the guilty ones are the leaders who were supposed to care for it and who rejected the Son. The ambush of Isaiah prepared the way for the ambush of Jesus, and in both cases the question is the same: where is the fruit that God is looking for?
